title: Dynamic Algorithms for Graph Coloring
venue: Proceedings of the ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA 2018), SIAM
key_finding: Gives fast dynamic algorithms that maintain a proper vertex colouring while edges are inserted and deleted: a randomized (Delta+1)-vertex colouring with O(log Delta) expected amortized update time, a deterministic algorithm with O(polylog Delta) amortized update time that uses slightly more than Delta+1 colours, and edge-colouring results.
limitations: Theoretical. The palette is tied to the maximum degree (about Delta+1 colours), which is far more than the fixed number of exam periods. The objective is update time, not the smallest number of recoloured vertices. No experiments.
algorithm: Randomized and deterministic dynamic (Delta+1)-vertex-colouring data structures (hierarchical decomposition)
notes: All draft fields confirmed via OpenAlex DOI lookup (OpenAlex labels the source 'Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics eBooks'). Abstract was reconstructed from the OpenAlex inverted index, and some words were lost in reconstruction.

title: Dynamic Graph Coloring
key_finding: Studies how many vertex recolourings are needed to keep a colouring proper when vertices and edges are inserted and deleted. One algorithm keeps an O(C d N^(1/d))-colouring with O(d) recolourings per update. The other keeps an O(C d)-colouring with O(d N^(1/d)) recolourings per update. Lower bound: any algorithm that keeps a c-colouring of a 2-colourable graph must recolour Omega(N^(2/(c(c-1)))) vertices per update.
limitations: Worst-case theory only. The number of colours grows with C and log N rather than staying within a fixed palette (periods). No experiments.
algorithm: Two recolouring-budgeted dynamic colouring algorithms (colours vs recolourings trade-off) plus lower bound

title: Improved Dynamic Graph Coloring
key_finding: Improves the Barba et al. trade-off between number of colours and recolourings per update. For example, it gives O(C beta log^2 n) colours with O(beta) recolourings when beta = O(1). It also gives a deterministic O(alpha log^2 n)-colouring with O(1) amortized update time for graphs of arboricity alpha.
limitations: Theoretical, with no experiments. Palette sizes are polylogarithmic, not a fixed small number of periods.
algorithm: Dynamic colouring with bounded recolourings per update; low out-degree orientation data structure
notes: Confirmed via OpenAlex. The article number in the draft ('art. 41') was not confirmed; OpenAlex gives pages 1-24. The abstract text returned by the tool was paraphrased, so the key finding is a summary.

title: Constant-time Dynamic (Δ+1)-Coloring
key_finding: Fully dynamic Las Vegas algorithm with constant expected amortized time per update that maintains a proper (Delta+1)-vertex colouring, based on random vertex ranks. It also shows that deciding Delta-colourability in a dynamic graph needs Omega(log n) time per operation.
limitations: Theory only. The (Delta+1) palette is not the timetable's fixed number of periods. It does not minimise the number of recoloured vertices.
algorithm: Random-rank-based dynamic (Delta+1)-colouring
notes: Confirmed via OpenAlex; the OA copy is the STACS 2020 conference version. The draft's 'art. 16' was not confirmed; OpenAlex gives pages 1-21.

title: Fully Dynamic (Δ+1)-Coloring in O(1) Update Time
key_finding: Randomized algorithm that maintains a (Delta+1)-colouring with O(1) amortized update time, both in expectation and with high probability. This improves the O(log Delta) bound of Bhattacharya et al. (SODA 2018) and builds on Solomon's dynamic maximal matching approach.
limitations: Theory only. The palette is degree-based, and there is no minimal-perturbation objective.
algorithm: Randomized dynamic (Delta+1)-colouring
notes: Confirmed via OpenAlex (closed access). The draft's 'art. 10' was not confirmed; OpenAlex gives pages 1-25.

title: Effective and efficient dynamic graph coloring
key_finding: Maintains a graph colouring incrementally as the graph changes. The goal is colour counts close to the best static heuristics at much lower cost. A colour-propagation method explores the two-hop neighbourhood of the changed region to decide which vertices to recolour, and an index on colour information bounds that exploration. Experiments on benchmark datasets show large efficiency gains.
limitations: Objective is colour count plus speed. It does not bound or minimise the number of recoloured vertices against a fixed palette. Large general graphs, not timetabling.
algorithm: Incremental colour propagation with index-based pruning

title: Tackling the edge dynamic graph colouring problem with and without future adjacency information
key_finding: For edge-dynamic graphs, proposes ways to turn the feasible colouring at time t into an initial colouring at t+1, for random changes and for changes with probabilistic future information. Methods: reset (recolour from scratch); pass the old colouring with its clashes to tabu search; uncolour clashing vertices; and solveClashes (build a partial proper colouring, reinsert vertices, colour the residual graph). The text defines a Kempe-chain interchange operator. Experiments show that reusing the previous colouring helps. Exam timetabling is named as a motivating application.
limitations: Minimises the number of colours by solving successive k-colouring problems. Per the full text, it does not measure how many vertices change colour between time steps (no stability or perturbation objective). Experiments use edge-dynamic random graphs (n=500), not timetabling or Toronto instances.
algorithm: Modification operators (reset, calculateClashes, uncolourClashes, solveClashes) feeding TabuCol-style tabu search; Kempe-chain interchange
notes: Year corrected to 2017: OpenAlex publication_year is 2017 (online first). The draft's 2018 likely refers to the volume 24(3) issue date, which was not confirmed here. The full text was read via the Springer fulltext page with targeted questions. Answers came through the WebFetch summariser and are not verbatim except the Kempe-chain quote.

title: Trade-Offs in Dynamic Coloring for Bipartite and General Graphs
key_finding: Studies trade-offs between update time, query time and recolourings per update. For general graphs it gives deterministic algorithms with a constant number of recolourings per update. For bipartite graphs it proves a lower bound of Omega(log n) amortized recolourings for keeping a 2-colouring. It gets around this bound with more colours or with implicit colouring, giving near-constant update and query time for incremental colouring.
limitations: Theoretical. Palette is not fixed to a given number of periods. No timetabling experiments.
algorithm: Deterministic dynamic colouring data structures; implicit colouring for bipartite graphs

title: Recoloring Interval Graphs with Limited Recourse Budget
venue: Scandinavian Symposium and Workshops on Algorithm Theory (SWAT 2020), LIPIcs
key_finding: Intervals arrive one at a time and must be coloured immediately, with only a limited number of recolourings (the recourse budget) allowed per step. Results: a 2k-colouring with amortized O(log n) recourse; a k-colouring with O(k*k!*sqrt(n)) recourse; for unit interval graphs, a (k+1)-colouring with O(k^2) worst-case recourse; and an Omega(log n) lower bound for maintaining a k-colouring.
limitations: Interval graphs only (not general conflict graphs). Vertex arrivals, not edge insertions between existing vertices. Theoretical.
algorithm: Recourse-budgeted online/dynamic interval-graph colouring
notes: Title, authors, DOI and year were confirmed via OpenAlex. title: Integer programming for minimal perturbation problems in university course timetabling
key_finding: Presents a general integer-programming approach to the minimal perturbation problem in university course timetabling. The setting is an existing timetable that has hard-constraint violations, explicitly including those caused by unexpected changes to course enrolments or rooms. Each infeasibility is resolved in the smallest possible neighbourhood using exact IP, which keeps computation fast and prevents large, disruptive event moves. Demonstrated on real University of Auckland data.
limitations: Course (not exam) timetabling. Exact IP on growing neighbourhoods rather than graph-colouring move operators. Evaluated on one university's data, not Toronto benchmarks.
algorithm: IP-based minimal-perturbation repair with expanding neighbourhoods
notes: Confirmed via OpenAlex and the Springer page. Window status is borderline: published online 2016-01-07 (before the 2016-10-04 window start), issue dated May 2017 (inside the window). The year shown is the issue year. OpenAlex has no abstract, so the abstract is taken verbatim from the Springer page. This is the closest match in motivation: enrolment changes leading to minimal-perturbation repair.

title: Disruptions in timetables: a case study at Universidade de Lisboa
key_finding: Addresses the minimal perturbation problem in university course timetabling: given disruptions that make a timetable infeasible, find the closest feasible timetable. It proposes two integer programming models. Disruptions are generated from probability distributions learned from five years of timetables at IST (Universidade de Lisboa). With an incremental approach, the models solve all instances.
limitations: Course timetabling (Springer page confirms not exam). Exact IP. Single-institution data.
algorithm: Two IP models for MPP, solved incrementally

title: Minimum penalty perturbation heuristics for curriculum-based timetables subject to multiple disruptions
key_finding: Repairs course timetables made infeasible by unexpected changes. It minimises quality degradation subject to an upper limit on the structural difference from the initial timetable, which is a perturbation budget. Proposes one simulated annealing algorithm and a set of IP-based algorithms. Tested on ITC-2007 curriculum-based instances with random disruption scenarios built from four disruption types that affect teacher and room availability. Also used to estimate solution robustness.
limitations: Curriculum-based course timetabling, not exams. Disruptions are availability changes (teacher/room), not new student-conflict edges. ITC-2007, not Toronto.

title: Robust university course timetabling problem subject to single and multiple disruptions
key_finding: Builds robust course timetables, where robustness means few changes are needed when disruptions occur. It defines single-disruption and multiple-disruption versions. Two multi-objective simulated annealing algorithms (MOSA-SD, MOSA-SAA) approximate Pareto fronts of soft-constraint penalty versus robustness. On ITC data, MOSA-SD beats a genetic algorithm, and MOSA-SAA does better under multiple disruptions, using a solution network for efficient evaluation.
limitations: Proactive robustness, not reactive repair. Course timetabling. ITC data.
algorithm: Multi-objective simulated annealing (MOSA-SD, MOSA-SAA)

title: On the computation of robust examination timetables: methods and experimental results
key_finding: Exam timetables often must be published before registration data are known. Using robustness techniques, exam timetables can be computed from curricula instead of registrations. Introduces three robustness measures for the resulting uncertainty and analyses them, with other quality metrics, using a multi-objective simulated annealing algorithm compared with Pareto-front approximations. A case study shows that, without significant loss of quality, the chance that rescheduling is needed once exact student numbers are known is significantly reduced.
limitations: Proactive (robust construction) rather than reactive repair. It does not propose a minimal-move repair algorithm for after enrolment changes. The case-study data are not named in the abstract; no evidence of Toronto instances.
algorithm: Multi-objective simulated annealing with three robustness measures

title: Time Complexity Analysis of Randomized Search Heuristics for the Dynamic Graph Coloring Problem
key_finding: Analyses the expected time for randomized search heuristics ((1+1) EA, RLS with a bounded palette minimising conflicts; iterated local search with an unbounded palette and a Kempe-chain mutation operator) to rediscover a proper or high-quality colouring after up to T edges are added. Edge deletions are ignored because they cannot worsen a colouring. For some bipartite graph classes, reoptimisation is as hard as or harder than optimising from scratch. Mutation operators tailored to where the changes occurred can greatly reduce the expected time.
limitations: Runtime theory on bipartite graphs (paths, binary trees, stars, general bipartite) and planar graphs with maximum degree at most 6. The objective is time to restore a proper or optimal colouring, not minimising the number of recoloured vertices. No timetabling or Toronto instances.
algorithm: (1+1) EA, RLS, iterated local search with Kempe-chain mutation; tailored mutation near inserted edges

title: Fixing improper colorings of graphs
key_finding: Defines Color-Fixing: given a non-proper r-colouring of a graph, find a proper r-colouring that differs from it on as few vertices as possible. The problem is NP-complete for every r >= 3, even on bipartite planar graphs. It is fixed-parameter tractable in the number k of recoloured vertices. Other results: a 2^n n^O(1) exact algorithm, a linear algorithm for bounded treewidth, lower bounds under standard assumptions, and the notion of the 'fixing number' of a graph.
limitations: Theory only, with no experiments or timetabling application.
algorithm: Exact exponential and FPT algorithms; hardness proofs
notes: Metadata confirmed via OpenAlex (publication_year 2017, online first; the volume-711 issue year was not confirmed). title: Shortest Reconfiguration of Colorings Under Kempe Changes
venue: Symposium on Theoretical Aspects of Computer Science (STACS 2020), LIPIcs
key_finding: A Kempe change swaps the two colours on a bicoloured connected component. The paper studies the complexity of finding the fewest Kempe changes that transform one given k-colouring into another. It admits a (highly non-trivial) polynomial-time dynamic program on paths. It is NP-hard even on star graphs, yet has a constant-factor approximation and is fixed-parameter tractable in k.
limitations: Theory on restricted graph classes. The objective is the number of Kempe changes between two given proper colourings, not repair after edge insertion.
algorithm: Dynamic programming on paths; approximation and FPT algorithms via canonical transformations

title: Kempe changes in degenerate graphs
key_finding: In (k-1)-degenerate graphs all k-colourings are Kempe-equivalent, but the known sequences can be exponentially long. If treewidth is at most k-1, any two k-colourings are equivalent within O(k n^2) Kempe changes. For maximum degree Delta, Delta-colourings are equivalent within O(n^2) Kempe changes, unless Delta = 3 and a component is a 3-prism.
limitations: Pure graph theory. Polynomial bounds on sequence length, not algorithms for minimal repair.
notes: Metadata from OpenAlex (publication_year 2023, online first; the year of volume 119 was not confirmed). The abstract comes from the OpenAlex record of the arXiv version (10.48550/arxiv.2112.02313). Useful for justifying that Kempe interchanges can connect colourings within a fixed palette.
